Photograph: Michael Buholzer/EPA View image in fullscreen Police officers with an armoured vehicle respond to the shooting in Aarau in Switzerland. Photograph: Michael Buholzer/EPA Switzerland One person killed and five wounded in shooting at rave party in Switzerland, police say Major police response after several people hit by gunfire in incident west of Zurich Agence France-Presse Sun 30 Aug 2026 02.42 EDT Last modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 05.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google One person has been killed and five others wounded in a shooting at a rave party in northern Switzerland , local police said on Sunday. “The search for the perpetrators, whose identities are currently unknown, is under way,” they said on X, adding that the motives and exact circumstances were not yet known. The incident happened in Aarau, west of Zurich, prompting a “large-scale” police response, officers said on X. Swiss newspaper Blick reported on its website that the shots were fired before 3am on the sidelines of the Aarauer Rave. About 3,500 people attended the annual techno party between 3pm on Saturday and 2am on Sunday. View image in fullscreen Police officers patrol a street in downtown Aarau on Sunday. Photograph: Michael Buholzer/EPA Police spokesperson Vanessa Rumpold was quoted as telling the newspaper that the shooting happened at the racecourse where the event was held. “Several shots were fired within a large group of people,” she added. One witness reported “bursts of gunfire”. Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAP View image in fullscreen Police officers at the scene of a fatal shooting in Merrylands West. Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAP Sydney Fatal Sydney shooting could be another case of mistaken identity, police say A man shot dead in Merrylands West was not known to police, in a case with similarities to Tuesday’s killing in Campbelltown Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Achol Arok Wed 2 Sep 2026 06.32 EDT Last modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 07.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google New South Wales police are investigating the shooting death of a man in Sydney’s west as a potential case of mistaken identity, marking the second fatal shooting incident in as many days. Emergency services responded to reports of a shooting at a home in Merrylands West at about 3.15pm on Wednesday, where a man believed to be in his 30s sustained a gunshot wound. The victim, who was yet to be formally identified, was treated by paramedics but died at the scene. Police said the property was a location known to police for organised crime, but said “the victim has no links that we’re aware of to organised crime”. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email At a press conference, Supt Simon Glasser said it was unclear what the man who was shot was doing at the location or his connection to the residents. “The person who we believe has been shot has no adverse holdings with police. People that are linked to this address are known to … organised crime,” he said. “It’s very early on in the investigation, however, there is a possibility that the wrong person has been shot by these offenders.” The alleged shooting marks the second incident of its kind this week. Sydney home invasion during which man shot and killed a ‘targeted attack’, police believe Read more On Tuesday, 23-year-old Marco Tapia was shot dead in his bed as his family slept at about 3.40am after multiple attackers were believed to have forced their way into a two-storey home in Glen Alpine, near Campbelltown, in south-west Sydney. That case was being investigated as a case of mistaken identity, police said, because Tapia was not known to authorities and had nothing more than a traffic offence on his record. His martial arts gym remembered him in a public tribute overnight. “We lost a real one today,” they wrote, adding: “Rest easy Marco, one of us forever.” The Alameddine network, a notorious crime family, and the Coconut Cartel, an emerging crime-for-hire network, have allegedly become embroiled in a feud, spilling into shootings across Sydney in recent months. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Acting Supt Gretchen Atkins of Campbelltown police said on Tuesday she was aware of online posts about the Glen Alpine case and said everything was under consideration. The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said the incidents showed gangland violence was out of control. “We need to be very clear about the threat on our streets and that is dangerous organised criminals … innocent people have been in the firing line way too often,” she said. “Whether it is a young man, a student sleeping in his bed at night [or] a grandfather who’s kidnapped and murdered,” referring to the Sydney grandfather Chris Baghsarian , who was taken from his home on 13 February and later found dead. She suggested the government was not doing enough to stop the shootings. But the police minister, Yasmin Catley, criticised Sloane, whose electorate is in Sydney’s eastern suburbs, over her position on the state’s gun buyback scheme, launched after December’s Bondi massacre. “The member for Vaucluse, we must remember, is also the same person that wants to squash [national gun buyback reform],” Catley said. “She wants more guns on the street and wants to blame the police for not doing their job … I’m not tolerating that, I won’t have a bar of that.” Explore more on these topics Sydney New South Wales news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: FBI officials at the Cape Town international airport during the extradition process of suspected Black Axe members in South Africa on 11 September 2026. Photograph: Esa Alexander/Reuters View image in fullscreen FBI officials at the Cape Town international airport during the extradition process of suspected Black Axe members in South Africa on 11 September 2026. Photograph: Esa Alexander/Reuters FBI Six Nigerians extradited to US over $6M online romance scam Alleged members of Black Axe criminal network that swindled US women out of $6m flown from South Africa Guardian staff and Associated Press Sat 12 Sep 2026 10.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Six Nigerian nationals linked to an organized criminal network that allegedly swindled American women out of more than $6m through online romance scams were extradited to the United States on Friday. South African police confirmed they were to be extradited earlier on Friday, while local news in Africa confirmed that the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation, known as the Hawks, facilitated their handover to officials from the US Federal Bureau of Investigation and Secret Service at Cape Town international airport, in collaboration with Interpol South Africa. The men, who were arrested in the South African city of Cape Town in 2021, face wire fraud and money laundering charges. They are accused of belonging to a criminal network known as the Black Axe , which Interpol describes as being among criminal groups responsible for a significant share of the world’s cyber-enabled financial fraud, typically through romance, cryptocurrency and investment scams. According to South African police, the men are alleged to have targeted more than 100 women in the US, defrauding them of more than $6m through online romance or love scams. Among the alleged victims were pensioners and businesspeople who were reportedly targeted through sophisticated online relationships. “Through the coordination of Interpol South Africa, the six will today be transported from a correctional facility in Cape Town to Cape Town international airport, where they will be handed over to officials from the FBI and the United States Secret Service, who arrived in South Africa this morning,” said police spokesperson Katlego Mogale. A recent operation by Interpol targeting west African organized crime groups led to the arrest of 58 people and the identification of 263 suspects linked to various criminal networks involved in similar crimes, the multinational police body said last month. The operation aimed to disrupt money laundering, identify high-value targets, seize assets, and support arrests and prosecution. In South Africa , authorities raided seven locations in the city of Johannesburg linked to a syndicate that ran romance and investment scams targeting retirees in English-speaking countries. In that operation in South Africa, police arrested 39 people, seized $2.67m and froze more than 250 bank accounts, Interpol said. http://www.jpost.com/israel-news/culture.text: When actress and artist Lisa Edelstein met her now-husband, artist Robert Russell, he came with a deep desire to rediscover his Jewish identity and pass it on to his sons from a former marriage, then three and five. He found the perfect partner for the job in Lisa.In addition to being Jewish, Lisa has played numerous Jewish women, including Dr. Cuddy on House, the lead (and a producer) of Bravo's Girlfriends' Guide to Divorce, and the adult daughter of Alan Arkin's character on Netflix's The Kominsky Method.Now she's playing the matriarch anchoring Long Story Short, Netflix's time-shifting adult animated series about three generations of a Jewish family.The following is a blend of a written and a Zoom interview. She was warm, funny, and thoughtful.Lisa grew up Conservative and kosher, building sukkahs and sitting through four-hour Seders, attending synagogue on Saturdays and Hebrew school until she was sixteen. Shabbat dinner was non-negotiable. “My father would usually give a very simple Parsha,” she told me. “I didn't know that's what he was doing at the time. I just knew that every week he talked about the Torah portion. And that continued for my whole childhood.”Edelstein's Jewish rootsHER GRANDPARENTS were immigrants, their first language Yiddish. Pogroms and war had scattered the family. Some cousins went to America, but many more ended up in Argentina and Israel.Her father's Aunt Leah founded Kibbutz Daliya in the early 1900s. “They turned the rocky, dry land into a forest and farm and hosted dance festivals once a year. That part of the family is still there, although some of their descendants have left the kibbutz.”Other family members live in Tel Aviv, Herzliya, Nir Zvi, Haifa, and by the border of Lebanon. Her last visit was a few days after the last living Oct. 7 hostages came home. “Israel is a beautiful, messy, complicated, diverse, loud, funny, tragic, amazing, gorgeous, powerful country, and I'm grateful for its existence.”She drifted away from Jewish traditions in her young adulthood, but meeting her husband – and his own Jewish journey – pulled her back in. “When we met, it was pretty apparent to both of us that we were going to stay together forever, and so we created a home. The boys were going back and forth 50/50 between our household and their mom's, and we wanted to find a way to give them a joyous Jewish experience in this house.”Their solution was a “hip-hop Shabbat” with dance lessons from an instructor followed by a big Shabbat dinner. When the boys outgrew hip-hop, it became Shabbat Dungeons & Dragons: friends over for dinner, then up half the night immersed in the fantasy tabletop game. The boys have since graduated high school, but the joyous Shabbat dinner tradition continues at the Edelstein-Russell household, now with dozens of friends and family members.ALTHOUGH SHE grew up in a Jewish neighborhood, Lisa got a taste of antisemitism and “otherism” at an early age. Her family moved to Wayne, a Jewish enclave in New Jersey, in 1967 – the same year the Civil Rights Act finally forced the town to take down the “No Negroes, no Jews, no dogs allowed” signs in shop and restaurant windows.During a re-election campaign, the head of the school board claimed that the Jew running against him was going to cancel Christmas. In response to this outlandish charge, The New York Times dubbed the town “The Home of Antisemitism in the United States of America.”“He won the election, by the way, and then he became mayor for 12 years. So that guy was running my town in one way or another during my entire childhood there,” Lisa said.Her feelings of otherism, however, “weren't because someone pointed at me and yelled JEW,” she explained. “It was our culture, in general, that somehow accepted the idea that Jewish women were spoiled princesses that only cared about Bloomingdale's … that they had big noses and frizzy hair and were grating.”I remember the jokes and the moniker Jewish American Princess, with its derisive acronym JAP. Jokes like, “What does a Jewish American Princess make for dinner? A reservation.” And, “How do you tickle a Jewish American Princess? Gucci, Gucci, goo.”“I didn't want to own that stereotype,” she continued. “And I guess on some level, I believed that that was true because that was what I was being told, and so I felt shame around my Jewish identity.”When Lisa left home to study drama at New York University, she made a concerted effort to separate herself from that unpleasant association. “I felt like it was a part of myself I had to grow out of or away from, or somehow bury or erase.”Edelstein's reinvention and journey of self-explorationTHAT REINVENTION, and an explosion of self-exploration, led her into the New York City club scene and a walk on the wild side. She became so well known in the clubs that famed journalist Maureen Dowd wrote a feature about her in The New York Times titled “Lisa in Wonderland.”Dowd painted a colorful picture of the full-time drama student and celebutante: “She talks fast, walks fast, laughs often. Her stride is a fast-motion version of Marilyn Monroe's bouncy gait. Everything about her, from her vivid alto to her mane of brown curls, seems to vibrate.”Lisa immersed herself in a world of experimental theater and experimental human beings. “It was the most exciting and diverse group of creative people I'd ever seen,” she said of the club life. “I couldn't get enough of how weird and wonderful and psychedelic the city could be. I learned an enormous amount, met incredible people, and was immersed in a community bursting with imagination and juice. So it was more than just fun for me; it was me finding out what excited me, what surprised me, even what terrified me.”In the club scene, she went by Lisa E, unsure how to “own a name like Edelstein out in the world without having to constantly battle with the preconceived idea of what that meant.” In time, she realized the stereotype had nothing to do with her.Writing an AIDS-related musical, Positive Me, forced a decision: Lisa E, or Lisa Edelstein, on the poster? “Am I moving forward as myself, or am I moving forward as this creation?”She decided she couldn't leave herself behind. Changing her name felt like “Hitler would win. Like I was abandoning my people and my heritage and my ancestors. I started to realize, you have to find a way to carry yourself with you, despite what people might think.”For decades, Jewish actors anglicized their names. Woody Allen was born Allan Stewart Konigsberg. Peter Coyote was Robert Peter Cohon. Winona Ryder changed her name from Winona Horowitz. And Albert Brooks was born Albert Einstein. Okay, you can't blame him for that one.JOINING THE Screen Actors Guild, Lisa said, marked another milestone. Was she worried about typecasting?“The answer is yes, and for sure it got in my way. I had several experiences where producers would call me crying or tell me years later that they were not allowed to cast me because I was too Jewish. If I had changed my name, maybe that wouldn't have happened. Who knows? I got jobs anyway, and a lot of those characters became Jewish without my trying, because people saw me that way, so that's fine.”That's more than fine with me. The casting of non-Jewish actors in Jewish roles, a rare practice today for other marginalized groups, remains ubiquitous in Hollywood. I don't love the idea of artificially restricting actors who can convincingly play other ethnicities, but if we are calling for authenticity for other minorities, we should do the same for Jews. Lisa has also portrayed many Jewish mothers, so I asked her to describe her mother. “HA!” she playfully responded, “describe YOUR mother.” I didn't, but Lisa did.Bonnie Edelstein graduated high school at 16 and married at 19. She's tough, critical, deeply opinionated, “confused by technology but offended by that confusion,” and loves playing solitaire on her phone.Bonnie's mother, Grandma Gertie, was one of Lisa's favorite people – an unstoppable force of hilarity and attitude. “She smoked two packs of cigarettes for 70 years and then gave it up in a day. She was the president of the sisterhoods of five different synagogues in Coney Island and Brighton Beach.”Both women fed directly into Lisa's performance as the matriarch of Long Story Short, Naomi – a feisty, witty woman unafraid to pick a fight over something that matters to her. She loves her family the best way she knows how, but she still gets under the skin of her three kids. Lisa admitted Naomi leans toward the stereotypical “cloying Jewish mom,” but believes it's those very expectations that trick the audience into falling in love with her.In a second-season twist, we learn, right alongside her children, that she's beloved by the wider community and a heroine to many. It strikes me that in families, we're all playing roles. Whether you're the provider, the nurturer, the rebel, or the complainer, we get locked into those parts, and it keeps the people closest to us from ever fully knowing who we are.Edelstein explores hidden histories in Little BirdTHAT THEME of hidden histories carries into another project of Lisa's: Little Bird, a six-episode Canadian miniseries about the “Sixties Scoop,” when government policy tore Indigenous children from their families to be raised in foster care or adopted into non-Indigenous homes, cut off from their culture. Adoptive parents believed they were rescuing abandoned children, not participating in a kidnapping scheme.Lisa plays Golda Rosenbaum, a Holocaust survivor who immigrated from Poland to Montreal and adopted a young Saskatchewan girl, raising her as a Jew and renaming her Esther. “Golda thinks she's raising somebody who she shares the experience with of having lost their families,” Lisa explained. “She adopts her when she's 5, and by the time her daughter is 25 and ready to get married, her daughter cannot move forward without finding out what actually happened to her.” So Esther sets off in search of her Indigenous family.When a member of her Indigenous family dies, Esther processes her grief through both traditions. Lisa and I talked about how ritual and tradition help us process events and regulate our emotions. “No one does mourning better than Jews,” Lisa opined. “We've got a guidebook like no other guidebook. There's a written plan about how you walk through this tragedy in your life, and it's beautiful.”Jewish characters are rare in film and television outside stories with intrinsically Jewish storylines. Yet, Lisa made her Abby in Girlfriends' Guide to Divorce, a show about a recent divorcee going through a common modern experience, a member of the tribe. “That was a dream job. One that I'm so glad I got to experience while I could still wear really, really high heels for any length of time. To get to be funny and sexy, smart, and emotional all in one job was deeply fulfilling,” she said.Edelstein's impulse to createLISA STARTED PAINTING as an extension of a lifelong impulse to create, transforming what she once viewed as a private coping mechanism into an applauded second career. “My husband gave me a painting on our second date, and asked me for a drawing in return,” she shared. Exchanging handmade gifts gradually became central to their relationship, helping her recognize that “that part of myself was valuable.”The turning point came when COVID slowed the world. Looking for a subject for her artwork, Edelstein immersed herself in family photographs she inherited after helping her parents downsize. She discovered “so many stories, so many memories, so many things I didn't remember,” and decided “to make myself a coloring book out of these images.”What began with magic markers evolved into increasingly intricate works. When friends urged her to abandon markers for paint, she switched to watercolor, opening new creative possibilities. She worked obsessively – sometimes “6 hours, 10 hours” – and found the experience exhilarating. Since then, she has moved into oils and mounted four exhibitions, with two works entering museum collections. “It's been a really magical journey,” she told me.I was struck by the paintings' vivid colors and dense patterns, which evoked their eras without overshadowing the people. Edelstein explained that her early reliance on markers naturally led her to seek photographs rich with pattern, making the 1970s of her youth “just a gift.” Although her source material now spans about 100 years, she unifies work with a consistent palette.“Mostly what I'm looking for in these images is narrative,” Edelstein said. She is drawn to photographs that “accidentally tell a story,” revealing something unexpected about a person's character or life. Carefully posed family portraits rarely interest her.One of my favorite paintings is Vampirella, a portrait of Lisa at eleven, in glasses and a nightgown, surrounded by the intimate clutter of her bedroom. Another painting that stays with me is Celebration, which bursts with affection and movement. Lisa believes the original photo was one of her grandparents' wedding anniversaries. What captivates her is not the event but the exuberant humanity within it: “There's just so much momentum, there's so many stories in that image.”I am struck by the family dynamics – fathers and daughters, husbands and wives – and by the many yarmulkes. Edelstein explained that the visible Jewish identity in her work became an intentional artistic choice even before the Oct. 7, 2023 massacre of innocent Israelis and visitors by Hamas.The impact of Oct. 7 on Edelstein's Jewish identityWhen preparing for her first gallery show, she remembered being asked, “Are you sure you want to go this Jew-forward?”“Well, yeah, it's my family. We are also a minority,” she said, “and we have a rich culture in this country [USA].” After Oct. 7, that commitment deepened, and since then, she has made sure every exhibition includes work reflecting Jewish life and culture.LIKE MOST JEWS, Lisa and Robert were devastated by the attack, but the reactions from friends were mixed. “We have a few friends who cried with us, who checked in frequently, who never stopped wanting to talk about what happened and what we have all been going through,” she said. On the other hand, “We had to end a few friendships completely because they were total dead ends. It has been painful and sad and also made us furious.”While the hostages were still being held captive, Lisa wore a Star of David she bought during a visit to Israel in the 70s along with a yellow ribbon hostage pin. At work, a colleague referenced the star and pin, saying, “It seems like you're making a very political statement. Are you sure you want to do that?”“A Jewish person said this to me!” an exasperated Lisa told me. “It doesn't matter what statement people think I'm making by wearing this,” she told her colleague. “It matters that they know who they're talking to, and edit accordingly.”And then there was the silence. “I confronted one of our friends post-Oct. 7. I felt she'd let her politics get in the way of her empathy when she didn't even bother to check in with us after such a traumatizing event. Her excuse surprised me: she had no idea we would care about what was happening there. She had no idea that Jewish people feel connected to each other,” Lisa shared.“She was shocked to be confronted, and I was shocked to realize that this was something completely unique to us. We are a people. We feel each other's successes and failures, triumphs, and tragedies. Some of us are annoyed by 'others of us,' but we are still, somehow, an 'Us.' And that isn't something most people experience or comprehend. It makes us incredibly special.” ■Lana Melman is an attorney and 20-year entertainment veteran, the CEO of Liberate Art, and the author of the award-winning book Artists Under Fire: The BDS War Against Celebrities, Jews, and Israel. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Yemeni military reinforcements travel along the coastal road between Aden and Mocha, Yemen, on Monday. Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP View image in fullscreen Yemeni military reinforcements travel along the coastal road between Aden and Mocha, Yemen, on Monday. Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP Yemen Air campaign against Houthis under way in Yemen, says Saudi-led coalition Operation supported by 100 fighter jets said to have secured ‘air protection’ of Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of targets Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Mon 5 Oct 2026 11.21 EDT Last modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 18.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Leaders of a Saudi-led coalition in Yemen claimed a broad air campaign involving 100 jet aircraft was under way on Monday against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coastline and farther north in the capital, Sana’a. The Saudi coalition spokesperson, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the 100 fighter jets participating in Operation Dawn of Yemen were providing support to forces of Yemen’s internationally recognised government. He said the coalition had secured “air protection” of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets. He claimed hundreds of Houthi fighters had been besieged in the Dhubab district, including the airport, close to the Bab al-Mandab strait, with some Houthi fighters fleeing across the Red Sea in boats. View image in fullscreen A man inspects the damage at a factory in Sana’a that was hit by an airstrike on Sunday. Photograph: Reuters Southern Yemeni forces known as the Giants Brigades, who are allied with the government, earlier on Monday launched a ground offensive against the rebels on the eastern flank of the coastal areas that the Houthis seized in their latest advances. The government forces also claim to have cut the road between Mocha and Dhubab, and that Houthi forces were deserting the recently captured city of Mocha as residents stayed behind closed doors. Previous Saudi-led statements about territorial gains in recent weeks have often proved partial, but footage appeared to back up the Saudi claims of Houthis retreating by the seashore. The president of the Saudi-backed government, Rashad al-Alimi, had promised a new offensive on Sunday, saying patience with the Houthis had run out. “Today we are embarking on a decisive phase in the history of our nation,” he said. View image in fullscreen Smoke rises from the site of an airstrike in Sana’a on Sunday. Photograph: Reuters Airstrikes were also reported on Monday in Sana’a and the Houthi stronghold of Saada in the north of Yemen. Command and control centres, camps and weapons depots were targeted. The Houthis, who captured Sana’a in 2014, have in recent weeks made lightning advances down the west coast of Yemen, reaching the Bab al-Mandab and seizing strategic islands on the strait. On Monday Houthi sources denied reports of a retreat, and pointed to the explosions at a Saudi Aramco plant in Riyadh as a sign of the damage the group could still inflict on exposed Saudi oil installations, and by extension the world economy. View image in fullscreen Flames burn on Saturday at an oil facility south of Riyadh belonging to Saudi Aramco. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images It appears a political agreement reached between the two main external Arab actors in Yemen – Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – permitted the UAE-backed Southern Giants to coordinate with the Saudi air force in the attack towards the coast. It is being stressed by the Giants Brigades that no other ground forces supporting the Saudi-backed government are involved in the offensive. The brigades, who are linked with the Southern Transitional Council, a political group outlawed in Yemen for trying to set up a secessionist state , are certain to have sought political commitments about the future status of Yemen in order to have thrown their military weight behind it. It is not clear how the Saudis propose to address the age-old southern question. Concessions to the Southern Transitional Council (STC) about the future governance of the south are certain to have been demanded, even if the UAE itself does not return to Yemen. But the cooperation between the Saudi air force and the Giants Brigades is a remarkable turnaround, since as recently as January the Saudi air force was bombing UAE shipments of arms arriving in southern Yemen for STC-backed forces. The Saudi bombing triggered the UAE pullout from Yemen in January, the sudden dissolution of the STC, and the exile of its leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi. At the weekend his supporters vowed to hold demonstrations later this month in support of the return to a separate southern state. Houthi government officials claimed British fighter jets were supporting the Saudi air force with refuelling, something the UK Ministry of Defence has already announced . The fighting was under way as senior ministers from Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia met in Riyadh to discuss the support Saudi Arabia might need to protect itself from the Houthis. They have formed a joint defence pact but it is not known how it will operate. https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/world/a.text: Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages Search Search All Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages GO Home World News Paprika makers fight to save national spice AFP, Kalocsa, Hungary Add TT as Preferred Source Working from before dawn until midnight, farmers Nikoletta Pajsan Nagy and Laszlo Pajsan fought Europe’s driest summer ever to save their red pepper harvest in Hungary. Unable to irrigate much of their two-and-a-half-hectare land because power lines run across it, they repeatedly loosened the soil around the plants, which are used to make the central European country’s signature spice, paprika. “I was absolutely convinced that we’d have to take on part-time jobs because they’d burn out,” Pajsan Nagy, 44, said, while selling her family’s products at the annual town fair in Kalocsa, in southern Hungary. A customer tastes a paprika product during the Paprika and Gastronomy Festival in Kalocsa, Hungary, on Sept. 19. Photo: AFP “But somehow the crop turned out bigger and more beautiful than in previous years. It was a miracle,” she said, recalling some 20-hour days in the field. The couple see themselves as a dwindling profession, as cultivation of paprika — an indispensable ingredient in traditional cuisine — has declined over the past several decades in Hungary, with many small producers going out of business. The area devoted to paprika peaked at 13,029 hectares in 1979 and had fallen to 1,410 hectares by 2024, official statistics showed. While cheap imports from China and parts of South America are squeezing producers, climate change is making paprika production more difficult and costly, said Robert Braj, an adviser at Dutch-owned BWA Kft, one of Hungary’s top food-seasoning manufacturers. “There are longer droughts, more extreme heatwaves, while new pests and diseases are spreading,” Braj said. Along with some other EU nations, Hungary experienced its driest summer since records began in 1901 and its second-hottest on record, the national weather service HungaroMet said. Labor shortages are also a problem. At the fair, paprika seller Agnes Toth recalled picking up peppers as a child, taking part in the family business. “Back then, we grew paprika on six hectares. Now it’s around three hectares because there aren’t enough seasonal workers to harvest it by hand,” the 44-year-old said. “A family couldn’t make a living from this anymore... Everyone has a full-time job. I’m a teacher, my brother is a firefighter,” she said. Hungary’s Agriculture and Food Economy Ministry said it seeks to bolster producers’ competitiveness, but it is yet to announce any new measures. At last month’s annual fair in Kalocsa, one of Hungary’s main paprika-growing regions, the aroma of meat stews and fish soups laced with the vibrant scarlet spice filled the air as teams poured generous amounts into their cauldrons at a cooking contest. “For us Hungarians, paprika is a wonder,” one of the competitors, local fast-food restaurant owner Imre Zseni said, while stirring a beef stew. Booths were adorned with strings of dried red peppers — the raw ingredient used to make paprika — recalling a sight once common on houses in the surrounding countryside every autumn. Originating from the Americas, peppers found their way to Hungary’s sun-drenched, fertile river plains around Kalocsa and Szeged in the 16th century. The two historic paprika-production centers are recognized with the EU’s protected designation of origin status. Ethnographer Imre Romsics said paprika became an important symbol of Hungarian identity during the 19th century, “alongside costume, folk art and other traditions.” However, younger generations cook fewer traditional Hungarian recipes, and they prefer food “that is faster and easier to prepare,” specialist Braj said.
